passages.title: The Rain Barrel
passages.text: After a dry week, the garden soil turned pale and dusty. Sam rolled a wooden barrel under the shed roof just as clouds piled up in the west. Rain struck the barrel lid, then the path, then the thirsty beds. In the morning the barrel was heavy. Sam dipped a pail and watered the young beans first, then the tomatoes along the fence. The plants lifted their leaves. Sam learned that saving rain is a quiet kind of work: you prepare before the storm, and the garden drinks later.

passages.title: The Wren in the Gourd
passages.text: A dried gourd hung from the trellis, hollow and pale. In April a tiny wren slipped inside with a beak full of moss. Day after day she wove a nest no bigger than a fist. Sam did not tap the gourd. He sat on the path and watched from a distance. When four thin mouths opened in the dark opening, the wren brought moths and beetles from the compost heap. The garden was not only food for people. It was a kitchen for a bird family, too.

passages.title: Workers in the Heap
passages.text: The compost heap looked like a pile of scraps: apple cores, bean vines, and last week's grass. Under the top layer the heap was warm. Red worms pulled bits of leaf into dark tunnels. Jane turned the pile with a fork once a week so air could reach the middle. In autumn she spread the finished compost along the furrows. The soil smelled sweet, not rotten. Jane told her brother that worms do not need thanks, but the garden pays them anyway with softer ground and stronger roots.

passages.title: The Last Tomato
passages.text: By late season only one tomato still hung on the vine, heavy and red. Mark had planned to carry it home for supper. Then he saw a neighbor pause at the fence with an empty basket. The neighbor had given Mark extra bean starts in spring. Mark picked the tomato, wiped the dust on his sleeve, and set it in the basket. Supper that night was beans and bread, not tomato, but the table felt full. In a garden, harvest is not only what you keep. It is also what you pass along.
